meta.title: Who really said "I think our society is run by insane people for insane objectives"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine. John Lennon said it to Peter Lewis for BBC 2's Release, recorded 6 June 1968 — and quote sites quietly delete his opening "I think."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I think our society is run by insane people for insane objectives'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: John Lennon, BBC 2's Release, recorded 6 June 1968, interviewer Peter Lewis. Two transcripts match — but the popular version drops his "I think."

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Lennon said it, in exactly these words, to the journalist Peter Lewis in an interview recorded on 6 June 1968 for the BBC 2 arts programme Release, first broadcast on 22 June 1968. Two independent transcripts of that interview carry the sentence verbatim, and an abridged version was later printed in The Beatles Anthology.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Thursday 6 June 1968, EMI Studios, Abbey Road, London
Peter Lewis; Victor Spinetti also present

source.excerpt: I think our society is run by insane people for insane objectives. And I think that’s what I sussed when I was 16 and 12, way down the line. But I expressed it differently all through my life. … But now I can put it into that sentence that I think we’re being run by maniacs for maniacal ends, you know.
trail: The Beatles Bible ↗ transcribes the whole interview and states that it was recorded at EMI Studios on 6 June 1968 for the BBC 2 arts show Release, conducted by Peter Lewis and first broadcast at 10.05pm on 22 June.
A second, independently maintained transcript at the Beatles Interviews Database ↗ reproduces the same answer with the identical opening sentence — two texts, one wording.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line twice in its sourced Quotes section — once as the 6 June 1968 interview, once from The Beatles Anthology (2000) — and not under its Disputed or Misattributed headings.
The occasion checks out: Wikipedia ↗ confirms the National Theatre Company’s stage version of In His Own Write, adapted by Victor Spinetti and Adrienne Kennedy, opened at the Old Vic on 18 June 1968.
source.excerptNote: The ellipsis marks Lennon’s aside about expressing the same thing all his life. The Beatles Anthology (2000) prints a shorter form of the same answer, cutting straight from “insane objectives” to the “maniacs for maniacal ends” clause.

author.name: John Lennon
author.heading: About John Lennon
author.metaLine: 9 October 1940 – 8 December 1980 · English musician, songwriter and activist
author.bio: John Lennon was an English musician, songwriter and activist who found global fame as the founder, co-lead vocalist and rhythm guitarist of the Beatles. Alongside the songs he was a published writer — his nonsense collection In His Own Write appeared in 1964 — and it was a television interview about the stage version of that book, in June 1968, that produced this line. By then he was moving from wordplay towards open political statement, the register that would define his solo work.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost in transmission
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — Lennon really did say this. What goes wrong is everything around it: the hedge at the front, the source underneath, and the room he was sitting in.

items.why: BrainyQuote ↗ and Goodreads ↗ both open with “Our society is run by insane people for insane objectives.” In the transcript Lennon begins “I think our society is run by…” — the edit converts a man offering an opinion into a man announcing a fact.

Neither page names an interview, a programme, a broadcaster or a date; Goodreads ↗ adds that its quotations are submitted by users and are not verified. The line is perfectly real, but as published there it is unfalsifiable.

The National Theatre connection is the play: its company staged In His Own Write at the Old Vic. The Beatles Bible ↗ records that the interview itself was taped at EMI Studios on Abbey Road, with Victor Spinetti alongside him.

The book prints a condensed version that elides the middle of the answer and joins the two halves, as reproduced on Wikiquote ↗. It is a faithful abridgement rather than an error, but it is not what was broadcast.

misattribution.truthLine: What Lennon actually said, on tape: “I think our society is run by insane people for insane objectives… But now I can put it into that sentence that I think we’re being run by maniacs for maniacal ends” — BBC 2, Release, recorded 6 June 1968 ↗.

context.heading: Why it landed
lead: Lennon was on television to talk about a play — the National Theatre Company’s stage version of his 1964 nonsense book In His Own Write, which opened at the Old Vic on 18 June 1968. The interviewer asked whether the boy in the play, who hates school and organised religion, was really Lennon attacking those things. The answer started politely and then went somewhere else entirely.

What makes the passage worth preserving is what Lennon says next, which almost never travels with the famous sentence: that he expects to be called insane for saying it. He then turns to the camera and tells the audience that half of them are about to ask what on earth he is talking about — which is, in effect, the sentence pre-empting its own reception.
detailsBody: Per The Beatles Bible ↗, the conversation was recorded at EMI Studios on Abbey Road on 6 June 1968 — the same night the band were at work on the White Album — and the session did not finish until 2.45am. It was then cut into four parts and slotted between extracts from the stage play, which were filmed separately in a BBC studio on 21 June.

That editing explains a small oddity in the finished programme: Peter Lewis’s scene-setting introduction refers to the play having already opened, even though Lennon’s answers were taped before the first night. The framing was added for the 22 June transmission, which is also why the segment is so often described as an interview “at the National Theatre.”
context.pull: I am liable to be put away as insane for expressing that. That’s what is insane about it.
